title: Local Quantum Fault Tolerance Without Expansion
abstract: We study fault-tolerant quantum computation using a fixed, local error-correction rule and a geometrically simple code: the cubical $(d,d')$-Toric code with $d',d-d'\geq 2$, including the 4D Toric code. Under sufficiently weak local-stochastic Pauli noise, our construction uses noiseless, bounded-depth classical processing per physical time step. Its correction cycle acts only on the current syndrome, has constant depth, and is repeated unchanged during idle logical computation; it requires neither multiscale decoder states nor scale-dependent communication delays.   Our proof treats errors and syndromes as chains in a cubical complex, combining geometric shrinking under the sweep rule with a space--time explanation-tree argument inspired by Toom's theorem. It does not rely on expansion. We establish three results:   1.Explicit higher-dimensional sweep rule. We give a local algorithm for choosing sweep corrections on cubical $(d,d')$-Toric complexes, resolving the local-existence question of Kubica and Preskill.   2. Fault-tolerant computation. We prove a circuit-level threshold theorem for noisy sweep cycles interleaved with logical gates. In particular, the 4D Toric code admits a fixed, constant-depth syndrome-based correction cycle without a multiscale decoder or expansion-based encoding. We do not claim constant total-depth overhead.   3. Ideal decoding under local-stochastic noise. For an initial local-stochastic Pauli error of rate $p$ below threshold, $n^{d+1}$ noiseless sweep cycles recover the encoded state on a side-length-$n$ $(d,d')$-Toric code with probability at least $1-O(\operatorname{poly}(n))p^{Ω(n)}$, extending earlier guarantees for independent errors.
summary: This paper develops a method for fault-tolerant quantum computation using the Toric code that avoids the need for code expansion. It proves a threshold theorem showing that a simple, constant-depth syndrome correction cycle can effectively combat local-stochastic noise. This provides a geometrically simple and highly desirable framework for building scalable quantum computers.
main_problem: The paper addresses achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation using simple, local error-correction rules without relying on code expansion.
main_result: It establishes a circuit-level threshold theorem for the 4D Toric code, showing that a fixed, constant-depth syndrome-based correction cycle can recover the state under local-stochastic Pauli noise.
method: The proof utilizes a chain-complex viewpoint, combining geometric shrinking under a sweep rule with a space-time explanation-tree argument inspired by Toom's theorem.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using the cubical (d,d')-Toric code, analyzed in a circuit model subjected to local-stochastic Pauli noise.
key_observables: Logical failure probability, which is bounded by $O(	ext{poly}(w, \mu, n)) p^{\Omega(n)}$ for noise rate $p$ below a threshold.
important_parameters: Noise rate $p$, code dimensions $d, d'$, and lattice size $n$.
main_assumptions: The classical processing per time step is assumed noiseless and has bounded depth; the noise is local-stochastic Pauli noise.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates potential walls bounding a syndrome component in the (2, 1)-Toric code, emphasizing the use of geometric span over Hamming weight.
paper_structure: The paper presents three main results: an explicit higher-dimensional sweep rule, a circuit-level threshold theorem for noisy sweep cycles, and a proof of ideal decoding under local-stochastic noise.
why_interesting: The focus on fixed, constant-depth syndrome processing without expansion is a major theoretical advance for building practical, scalable quantum error correction protocols.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A graphical example of the maximal values of the potential walls. Here we consider the (2, 1)-Toric code, namely the bits are set on the edges where the Z-stabilizers (parity checks) are set on the vertices. The grid is a finite 6 × 6 patch of the infinite 2D plane. The edges marked in blue correspond to a bits assignment z. Each of the dashed lines marks the line of vertices whose Li value converges with the maximal value reached by a vertex in z. Moving into the infinite plane enables us to determine those lines and draw the triangle that bounds z.

Figure 2: Above: The application of a sweep-cycle, where the green faces represent the bits assignment z, and the blue edges correspond to unsatisfied checks ∂−z. The vertices witnessing a syndrome, namely belonging to ∂−z, are labeled as v1, v2, . . . , v8. Notice that the leftmost bottom-inner vertex is not witnessing a syndrome even though it belongs to z. Below: The Toom’s contour derived from the single computation layer that matches the cycle. Arrows are colored in blue, while forks are colored in green. Note that (v1, t + 1) doesn’t belong to the Toom’s contour (since v1 doesn’t see an unsatisfied check at time t + 1).

Figure 3: Here we consider a 2D Toric complex. We name the set of generators S = {g1, g2}, where g1 is the generator that sends us one step in the north direction, and g2 sends us in the east direction. For vertices v, u, w, we mark in blue three faces that are rooted at them.

Figure 4: An example of applying the sweep rule within the (3, 2)-Toric code. In the (3, 2)-Toric code, bits are placed on the squares and Z-stabilizers (parity checks) on the edges. The view is restricted to two vertices, u and v. On the left, the unsatisfied positive checks of u and v are highlighted in blue. On the right, the bits to be flipped are marked in green. Given the syndrome, vertex v flips one of its positive faces, whereas for u, there is no subset of positive faces that, when flipped, satisfies local checks. Therefore, u flips no bit.

Figure 5: Consider the (3, 2)-Toric code, with qubits and X-checks set on the 2- and 1-dimensional faces. In blue, we have a 2-dimensional chain where the vertex achieving the maximum of Ld+1, denoted by v, does not see any unsatisfied checks in its positive local view. The green faces represent a 2-dimensional chain, which is the reduced form of the blue. In particular, any local maximum of Ld+1 (vertices u and w) sees a non-trivial syndrome in its positive local view. Namely, the maximal points of Ld+1 in the chain are also the maximal points in the boundary ∂−.
